newsitem.title: GERMANY: East Berlin mulled selling Nazi-era Jewish stocks.
newsitem.headline: East Berlin mulled selling Nazi-era Jewish stocks.

text.p: East Germany's communist government once considered secretly selling off stocks it held that had been confiscated from Jewish investors during the Nazi era, Focus magazine reported on Monday.
From 1958 to 1969, an East Berlin banker discreetly tried to sell the stocks in the West with the help of Switzerland's small communist party, it said.

The communists found 28 million confiscated stock certificates after the war in the basement of the Reichsbank, the former central bank building in eastern Berlin that they made their central committee headquarters, the magazine said.
After reunification in 1990, the German government offered to return the stocks to their original owners but few came forward to claim them.
Feodor Riesche, who was later head of the German Trade Bank in East Berlin, made confidential reports on the secret project to East Germany's Stasi security police, Focus said.
These papers have recently been found in the archives of the Ministry for State Security.

It was not clear how many of the 28 million stocks had once belonged to Jewish investors. Focus said they were now worthless, although they might have some value for people who collect old share certificates.
On one of the reports, an East German official noted the communists could be badly embarrassed if they were found to be profiting from Nazi confiscations of Jewish property.
"If the deal fails and it gets out that the communist party is behind it, this could be used by enemy propaganda and badly damage the image of the party and East Germany," he wrote.
Focus said the project never made any money "except for a small "test sale' in Holland that brought in a few thousand marks".
